title: Applications of Trigonometry
learningObjective: Solve applications that require the use of trigonometry to find a side or angle.

faqs.question: Where do I start with a trigonometry word problem?
faqs.answer:
Start with a picture, not a formula. Sketch the situation and label what you know and what you want to find. Then look for the triangle hiding in the picture: is there a right angle (a wall, level ground, a horizontal line of sight), or do you just have three pieces of information about a triangle? Only then choose your tool — right-triangle trig from TE4, or the Law of Sines or Law of Cosines from TE5 — and finish by checking that your answer makes sense (faq-14).

Every application problem follows the same four moves — the picture always comes first.

faqs.question: What are the angle of elevation and the angle of depression?
faqs.answer:
Both angles are measured from a horizontal line, never from the vertical. The angle of elevation is the angle between the horizontal and your line of sight to something above you. The angle of depression is the angle between the horizontal and your line of sight to something below you. Which one a problem uses depends only on who is doing the looking.

Both angles are measured from a horizontal line. The observer looks up at the plane (angle of elevation, teal); the pilot looks down at the observer (angle of depression, orange).

faqs.question: Why are the angle of elevation and the angle of depression equal?
faqs.answer:
Draw a horizontal line at each end of the line of sight. Those two horizontals are parallel, and the line of sight is a transversal crossing both, so the two angles form a Z — and alternate interior angles are equal. That means the angle of depression from the top always equals the angle of elevation from the bottom. This is useful because the angle you're handed is often outside your triangle, but it has an equal twin inside it.

The two horizontal lines are parallel and the line of sight cuts across both, tracing a Z. The two angles inside the Z are equal, so the angle of depression equals the angle of elevation.

faqs.question: How do I know whether a problem needs right-triangle trig or the Law of Sines/Cosines?
faqs.answer:
Ask two questions in order. First: is there a right angle in the picture? If so, use the right-triangle tools from TE4. If not, ask whether you already hold a complete opposite pair — a given angle and the given side directly across from it. If yes, use the Law of Sines; if no (you have SAS or SSS information), use the Law of Cosines.

Two questions decide the method: first, is there a right angle? If not, do you already hold an angle and the side directly across from it?

faqs.question: What does it mean for a real situation (tides, a Ferris wheel) to be modeled by a sine or cosine function?
faqs.answer:
Anything that repeats on a regular cycle — tides, a Ferris wheel, daily temperature — can be described by a sine or cosine function. Three numbers describe the cycle: the midline (the middle value — a vertical shift from FN4), the amplitude (how far it swings above and below the midline, from PF1), and the period (how long one full cycle takes, also from PF1). Written as a model: \( y = A\sin(Bt) + D \) (or a cosine), where \( |A| \) is the amplitude, \( D \) is the midline, and the period is \( \dfrac{2\pi}{B} \).

The three numbers that describe any repeating cycle: the midline (the middle value), the amplitude (how far it swings above and below), and the period (how long one full cycle takes).

faqs.question: What do I do when the angle I need isn't inside the triangle (like a pilot's angle of descent)?
faqs.answer:
Look for a horizontal line through the observer. It's parallel to the ground, so the line of sight acts as a transversal, and the angle of descent equals the angle at the other end of the line of sight — which sits inside your right triangle (alternate interior angles, faq-3). Then use the sides you know with an inverse trig function.

The angle the pilot needs (θ, measured down from her horizontal) sits outside the triangle. Because the horizontal is parallel to the ground, the same θ appears inside the triangle at the runway.

Worked Example — right triangle

A plane at 40,000 ft is a horizontal distance of 750,000 ft from the runway. Height (opposite) \( = 40{,}000 \); horizontal distance (adjacent) \( = 750{,}000 \).

\( \tan\theta = \dfrac{40{,}000}{750{,}000} \)

\( \theta = \arctan\!\left(\dfrac{40{,}000}{750{,}000}\right) \approx 3.05° \)

faqs.question: How do I find a height from an angle of elevation and a horizontal distance (and remember the observer's height)?
faqs.answer:
The height you want is opposite the angle of elevation, and the horizontal distance is adjacent to it — that's the tangent ratio: \( \tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{distance}} \), so height \( = \) distance \( \times \tan\theta \). That gives the height above the observer's eye level, so add the height of the observer's eyes at the end. (Make sure your calculator is in degree mode.)

The tangent of the 70° angle of elevation gives the height above the observer's eyes (teal); the observer's eye height is then added on. (The eye height is exaggerated here so you can see it.)

Worked Example — right triangle

An observer 1.5 m tall stands 67 m from the Seattle Space Needle. The angle of elevation to the top is \( 70° \).

Height above eye level: \( 67\tan 70° \approx 184.1 \) m

Add the observer's height: \( 184.1 + 1.5 \approx 185.6 \) m — about 186 m to the nearest meter.

faqs.question: How do I find a horizontal distance from an angle of depression?
faqs.answer:
By faq-3, the angle of depression from the cliff equals the angle of elevation from the ship, so it appears inside the right triangle at the ship. The cliff height is opposite that angle and the distance you want is adjacent — tangent again, but this time the unknown is in the denominator, so you divide: \( x = \dfrac{380}{\tan 9°} \). A small angle means a long distance, so a result of about 2.4 km fits a 9° angle.

True to scale: a 380 m cliff and a 9° angle of depression put the ship far from shore (about 2,399 m). The same 9° appears as the angle of elevation from the ship back up to the cliff top.

Worked Example — right triangle

Standing on a cliff 380 m above the sea, Sean sees a ship at an angle of depression of \( 9° \).

\( \tan 9° = \dfrac{380}{x} \)

\( x = \dfrac{380}{\tan 9°} \approx 2{,}399 \) m

faqs.question: How do I find an unknown angle when I know two sides (like the ladder and the wall)?
faqs.answer:
Use an inverse trig function (PF3, TE4). Decide which ratio fits the two sides you know, relative to the angle you want, then take the inverse. Here the wall (13 ft) is opposite the angle at the ground and the ladder (14 ft) is the hypotenuse, so sine is the match.

Drawn to scale: a 14 ft ladder just reaches the top of a 13 ft wall. The wall is opposite the angle at the ground and the ladder is the hypotenuse — a job for sine.

Worked Example — right triangle

A 14-foot ladder reaches the top of a 13-foot wall.

\( \sin\theta = \dfrac{13}{14} \)

\( \theta = \arcsin\!\left(\dfrac{13}{14}\right) \approx 68° \)

faqs.question: How do I solve an application with a non-right triangle when I know two angles and a side (the two airplanes)?
faqs.answer:
There's no right angle, and you know an angle and the side across from it, so use the Law of Sines (TE5). Match each side with the angle directly across from it: the side from airplane A to the airport (20 mi) is across from the \( 50° \) angle, and the side we want (airplane B to the airport) is across from the \( 45° \) angle.

Two angles and the side between airplane A and the airport are known (true to scale). No right angle here — the unknown side (orange) is across from the 45° angle.

Worked Example — Law of Sines

Airplane A is 20 miles from the airport. The angle at A is \( 45° \) and the angle at B is \( 50° \). Let \( d \) be B's distance to the airport.

\( \dfrac{d}{\sin 45°} = \dfrac{20}{\sin 50°} \)

\( d = \dfrac{20\sin 45°}{\sin 50°} \approx 18.5 \) miles

faqs.question: How do I solve one when I know all three sides (the campers), and why does rounding early cause trouble?
faqs.answer:
Three sides and no angles means the Law of Cosines first, to find one angle. After that you hold a complete opposite pair, so the Law of Sines can find a second angle, and subtracting from \( 180° \) gives the third. Keep extra decimal places through every step: rounding in the middle can shift the final answer.

The campers' tents form a triangle with all three sides known (true to scale) and no right angle — each angle is at a different camper.

Worked Example — Law of Cosines, then Law of Sines

Carlos (across from the 175 ft side): \( \cos C = \dfrac{153^2+201^2-175^2}{2(153)(201)} = \dfrac{33{,}185}{61{,}506} \approx 0.5395 \), so \( C \approx 57.35° \).

Travis (across from the 153 ft side): \( \dfrac{\sin T}{153} = \dfrac{\sin 57.35°}{175} \) gives \( \sin T \approx 0.7362 \), so \( T \approx 47.40° \). (The other candidate, \( 132.6° \), is impossible — it would push the angle sum past \( 180° \).)

Jean: \( 180° - 57.35° - 47.40° \approx 75.25° \).

Rounding trap: if you round the first two angles to \( 57° \) and \( 47° \) before subtracting, Jean comes out as \( 76° \) — but the accurate value is \( 75.25° \), about \( 75° \).

faqs.question: How do I find the maximum, minimum, and period from a trig model like the tide equation?
faqs.answer:
Read the model like a recipe. For \( d(t) = 2 + \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) \): the constant \( 2 \) is the midline, the coefficient \( \tfrac{1}{2} \) in front of the sine is the amplitude, and the number multiplying \( t \) (here \( \tfrac{\pi}{6} \)) sets the period. Careful with notation: the sine applies to the whole product \( \tfrac{\pi}{6}t \), not just to \( \tfrac{\pi}{6} \).

The tide model d(t) = 2 + ½ sin(πt/6): the depth swings between 1.5 m and 2.5 m around a midline of 2 m, and one full tide cycle takes 12 hours.

Worked Example — reading a model

Maximum \( = \) midline \( + \) amplitude \( = 2 + \dfrac{1}{2} = 2.5 \) m (high tide)

Minimum \( = \) midline \( - \) amplitude \( = 2 - \dfrac{1}{2} = 1.5 \) m (low tide)

Period \( = \dfrac{2\pi}{\pi/6} = 12 \) hours, so there are \( \dfrac{24}{12} = 2 \) tide cycles in a day.

faqs.question: How do I build a sine or cosine model for something like a Ferris wheel?
How do I check that my answer is reasonable?
faqs.answer:
A few quick checks catch most mistakes. (1) In a right triangle the hypotenuse must be the longest side. (2) In any triangle the longest side is across from the largest angle and the shortest side is across from the smallest. (3) A triangle's angles add to \( 180° \) (a right triangle's two acute angles add to \( 90° \)). (4) Ask whether the size fits the story — a shallow \( 9° \) angle of depression should give a distance much larger than the cliff's height. (5) Make sure your calculator is in degree mode for degree problems. (6) Answer in a sentence with units.

A quick sanity check: the longest side is always across from the largest angle (orange), and the shortest side is across from the smallest angle (teal).

faqs.question: How does this section pull together TE4 and TE5?
faqs.answer:
TE6 introduces no new triangle formulas. Every problem here is one you already have the tools for — the new skill is recognizing which tool fits, and drawing the diagram that reveals it. The pilot, Space Needle, cliff, and ladder problems hide right triangles (TE4); the two airplanes and the campers are non-right triangles that need TE5's laws. The campers problem even uses both laws in a single solution.

TE6 introduces no new triangle math — it's about recognizing which of your tools fits the situation.

faqs.question: How does the periodic-modeling part connect to PF1 and FN4?
faqs.answer: The amplitude and period in the tide and Ferris wheel models are exactly PF1's amplitude and period, with period \( = \dfrac{2\pi}{B} \). The midline is FN4's vertical shift (the \( +2 \) or \( +61 \) added to the wave), and the Ferris wheel's upside-down cosine is FN4's vertical reflection (the negative sign in \( -60\cos \)). Nothing here is new — it's the same transformations, tied to a real situation.

faqs.question: Why do these applications matter beyond this course?
faqs.answer: Surveyors, pilots, navigators, architects, and engineers use exactly these tools to find heights, distances, and angles they can't measure directly: a building's height from the ground, the glide angle for a landing, the distance to a ship, or a position fixed from two bearings. The periodic models show up in tides, sound and light waves, seasonal temperatures, alternating current, and amusement-ride design.

guided.title: Practice Drawing the Diagram First
guided.prompt: I'm learning to solve trigonometry word problems. Give me a short word problem about a ladder, ramp, or shadow — but don't solve it. Ask me to describe the diagram I would draw, label what is known and unknown, and tell you which triangle and which tool I would use. Then let me solve it and check my work. Give me a few more problems of increasing difficulty.

guided.title: Practice Angles of Elevation and Depression
guided.prompt: I'm learning about angles of elevation and depression. Give me a problem where I'm given an angle of depression, which is outside the triangle, and ask me how to find the equal angle inside the triangle. Ask me to explain WHY the two angles are equal before I calculate anything. Then check my setup and my answer, and give me two more problems.

guided.title: Choose the Right Method
guided.prompt: I sometimes can't tell which tool a word problem needs. Give me several triangle application scenarios — some with a right angle, some without. For each one, ask me whether I would use right-triangle trig, the Law of Sines, or the Law of Cosines, and why, BEFORE I compute anything. Check my reasoning and help me with any I get wrong.

guided.title: Practice a Multi-Step Non-Right Triangle Problem
guided.prompt: I'm learning to solve a triangle when I know all three sides, like three people in tents a known distance apart. Walk me through using the Law of Cosines for the first angle, the Law of Sines for the second, and subtraction for the third. Then show me what goes wrong if I round the first two angles too early, and give me a similar problem to try.

guided.title: Practice Modeling a Periodic Situation
guided.prompt: I'm learning to model real cycles with sine or cosine. Give me a situation like a tide, a Ferris wheel, or daily temperature. Ask me to find the midline, amplitude, and period from the description, decide whether sine or cosine fits, and write the model. Then have me check it by plugging in t = 0 and t = half a period.

open.title: Create Your Own
open.prompt: Use the AI tool of your choice. Start by describing what you're confused about or curious about from Section TE6 (Applications of Trigonometry). Ask the AI to help you explore that idea. Share what you learned and what surprised you.
